newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian parliament resumes inquisition on Di Rupo.
newsitem.headline: Belgian parliament resumes inquisition on Di Rupo.

text.p: Deputy Belgian Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo, partially cleared of allegations he had sex with under-age boys, faces a new probe by his parliamentary peers on Tuesday.

The Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court and the only one capable of judging a minister, handed a special parliamentary commission a report on Monday into the original allegations against Di Rupo by a sole witness, rejecting them as baseless.

But the Brussels prosecutor who has been compiling the case against di Rupo, a French-speaking socialist, has already compiled another file of allegations -- this time anonymous -- and spoke on Monday of more to come.

The allegations against Di Rupo have served to undermine public confidence in Belgium's political and legal system, already weakened by an unrelated child sex and murder scandal and ensuing revelations of bungling by investigators.
Last month Marie-France Botte, a prominent child rights campaigner, appealed for calm in the face of what she said were hundreds of letters a day containing all sorts of denunciations.
A police hot line set up in August after the discovery of a paedophile ring has received thousands of calls -- some of them about Di Rupo, a homosexual.
A minister in the French-speaking regional government quit his job on Monday after allegations of paedophilia.
Jean-Pierre Grafe denied the allegations but said he could not work properly in the current climate.
The Cour de Cassation is due to hand in a report on the allegations against Grafe later on Tuesday.

Newspaper editorials said that if Grafe was innocent it was a scandal and a threat to democracy that unsubstantiated allegations had caused his downfall. However, if he was guilty, they said, then what value did that put on the word of a minister.

The parliamentary commission can decide to reject the allegations against Di Rupo, to uphold them and indict him or to ask for more investigations. Its decision must then go to parliament to be put to the vote.

The Di Rupo affair has been another nail in the coffin of Belgian public confidence that has been shaken since the arrest of rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two young girls and discovery of the bodies of four more.

In October more than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in support of the victims and their families in a demonstration that crossed the country's language divide and rapidly turned into a show of anger at the system.
The government has rushed through a series of legal reforms and the leaders of the main political parties on Saturday began a process that should lead to long-awaited political changes.
But that still may be too late for Di Rupo, even if parliament decides he has no case to answer.
Some of his peers have already judged him and called for his resignation on the grounds that a publicly-known homosexual should not hold high government office.
